summary: One of Australia's smallest and most remote national parks: the whole of North Keeling Island, a C-shaped coral atoll in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and the waters around it, 2,600 hectares in all. It is a strict nature reserve and one of the world's great red-footed booby colonies, with nesting green turtles and pristine reef. There are no public tours, and getting ashore through the surf is very difficult; most people know the park from the southern atoll.
story: North Keeling Island is a coral atoll two kilometres long and 1.3 kilometres wide, built, like the southern atoll of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, on an old volcanic seamount that rises 5,000 metres from the ocean floor. Radiocarbon dating puts the island at only 3,000 to 4,000 years old. It is low and flat, ringed by coral shingle on its windward south and east shores and by shingle and white sand on the sheltered side, around a lagoon no more than two metres deep. The lagoon once opened to the sea; in 2005 natural deposits closed the entrance, and plants and nesting seabirds have since taken it over.

Its forests are examples of the region's original vegetation, with species no longer found elsewhere in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and it is one of the few seabird colonies in the Indian Ocean free of feral cats and rats. Tall pisonia forest, with ironwood grown to the size of large trees, shelters tens of thousands of red-footed boobies, one of the world's largest populations, alongside frigatebirds, tropicbirds, masked boobies, white terns and the endemic Cocos buff-banded rail; 16 bird species breed here, the only seabird colony for 900 kilometres. At least 26 species of crab live in the forest and on the beaches, among them robber crabs, and green turtles nest on the shore. The reef around the island is in near-pristine condition, with 201 fish species recorded, including the Cocos angelfish.

No one has ever lived permanently on North Keeling: it is far from the main atoll, hard to land on and has no fresh water. Yet the Cocos-Malay people, descended mainly from workers brought to the Clunies-Ross family's coconut plantations, have a long connection with it. Their boats came for coconuts, ironwood and seabirds; in the late 19th century people with beriberi were housed here, and Malay graves remain near the southern shore. Between the wars workers stayed for up to two weeks at a time in long-houses by the lagoon, and the remains of the houses and a small-gauge railway survive.

On 9 November 1914, in one of the first naval battles of the First World War, HMAS Sydney caught the German cruiser SMS Emden after its men had seized the station on Direction Island, and forced it onto the reefs of North Keeling. Seabird hunting with guns and flails grew after the Second World War, until the Australian Government and the Cocos-Malay community agreed a moratorium in 1986. The Cocos (Keeling) Shire Council leased the island to the Commonwealth in January 1995, the park was proclaimed on 12 December 1995, and in 1996 it was listed as a Ramsar wetland of international importance.
howItWorks: Pulu Keeling, from the Cocos-Malay pulu, 'island', is a Commonwealth reserve under the EPBC Act. Parks Australia leases it from the Cocos-Malay community and manages it on behalf of the Shire Council and the Cocos-Malay population, with a ten-member Community Management Committee representing the local community, the Shire Council and the Director of National Parks. The island is zoned as a strict nature reserve under the IUCN's definitions, so most activities need a permit.

The park is not open to general visits. Its remoteness, rough seas and fringing reef make getting ashore very difficult; researchers who land must be accompanied by park staff, and there are no tours for the public. Permits are needed for any research, for commercial filming or photography, for running tours, and for scuba diving, surfing or recreational fishing in the park's waters; commercial fishing is never allowed. The wreck of SMS Emden, off the southern end of the island, can be dived with a permit. Anyone planning a visit should contact park staff on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands first.

Biosecurity matters above everything here. The island has no rats or cats, but yellow crazy ants have been found in its pisonia forests, and scale insects that kill pisonia canopies must be kept out. Seabirds, including the red-footed boobies once hunted here, are protected under the EPBC Act. The southern atoll, with flights from Perth, accommodation and tour operators offering birdwatching, diving, fishing and turtle watching, is the place to stay and to learn about the park.

sights.name: North Keeling Island
sights.note: The whole park on land: a C-shaped coral atoll around a shallow, now-closed lagoon, under pisonia forest full of nesting red-footed boobies. Landing only with park staff.

entrances: No public access; researchers land only with park staff
Cocos (Keeling) Islands Airport on West Island, in the southern atoll, with Virgin Australia flights from Perth twice a week
planYourVisit.reservations: There are no public tours to North Keeling Island. Contact Pulu Keeling National Park (+61 8 9162 7602, pulukeelingnationalpark@dcceew.gov.au) before planning any trip; post can take up to six weeks.
permits: Permits for research, commercial filming and photography, and tours or other commercial activity
Permits for scuba diving, including the SMS Emden wreck, surfing and recreational fishing in park waters; commercial fishing is prohibited
lodging: Accommodation in the southern atoll of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands

weather: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands lie in the tropical Indian Ocean about halfway between Australia and Sri Lanka, and North Keeling is exposed on all sides. Parks Australia's pages give no climate figures for the park; what decides any trip is the sea, since rough seas and the fringing reef make landing very difficult. Check conditions locally before any approved visit.
directions: Pulu Keeling is about 2,900 kilometres north-west of Perth. Virgin Australia flies twice a week from Perth to the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, landing on West Island in the southern atoll, where there are places to stay and local tour operators. North Keeling lies to the north across open sea, and there is no public transport or tour to it; approved visits are made only with park staff.

chronology.text: Alexander Hare settles the southern atoll; John Clunies-Ross follows the next year and recruits Malay workers for his coconut plantation.
On 9 November HMAS Sydney drives SMS Emden onto the reefs of North Keeling Island.
The Cocos (Keeling) Islands become an Australian territory.
The government and the Cocos-Malay community agree a moratorium on seabird hunting on North Keeling.
The Shire Council leases North Keeling to the Commonwealth, and the national park is proclaimed on 12 December.
The whole park is listed as a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention.
Natural deposits close the lagoon's entrance to the sea.

safety: Landing on North Keeling is dangerous: the island is surrounded by a fringing reef and rough seas, which is why access is only with park staff.
The island has no fresh water and no facilities of any kind.
Help is far away. Postal services can be delayed by up to six weeks; phone and email are the reliable ways to reach park staff.
regulations: No landing without park staff; there are no public tours.
Permits are required for research, commercial filming and photography, tours, scuba diving, surfing and recreational fishing; commercial fishing is never permitted.
All birds in the park are protected under the EPBC Act.
Strict biosecurity: nothing that could carry pests, ants, scale insects or disease may be brought to the island.
